newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-As grains rally, other commodities languish.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-As grains rally, other commodities languish.

text.p: Grain prices extended a rally on Monday with wheat soaring by the daily trading limit of 20 cents per bushel in Chicago futures pits on fears that a late cold snap would hit US crops.
A drought in Europe fuelled concerns.
Elsewhere in world commodity markets, however, although crude oil seemed to be finding a floor after a long slide, most prices tended to drift lower. Gold stayed in a range.

Speculative money that may have fled Wall Street in the latest shake-out in equities did not seem to be finding a home in commodities. Funds, in fact, were seen still as having to liquidate some long positions in the sector.

Freezing weather in the Great Plains of the United States pushed US wheat futures up by their 20-cent daily limit in electronic dealing early on Monday, and similar gains followed when Chicago opened for formal trading.
Chicago July soft red winter wheat reached $4.28-1/4 per bushel, worth around $162 per tonne on world markets and up from lows of around $140 per tonne seen earlier this year.
In France, hampered by early fears of drought after weeks without rain, prices for the crop to be harvested in three months' time rose up to three percent, grain dealers said.
In Australia futures for the next harvest added five percent on world supply concerns and dry weather at home. US maize and soybean prices were also dragged higher by wheat.

Crude oil prices appear to have found a floor around $18 a barrel for benchmark North Sea Brent Blend ahead of the cyclical rise in demand for gasoline during the US summer holdays.
Concern over Iran's diplomatic standoff with the European Union also has helped to arrest a 30 percent slide in crude prices over the last three months.
London Brent crude slumped $7 a barrel from just below $25 in early January to a recent nine-month low at $17.65. But Brent for May was trading around $18.20 in London's Monday afternoon.
Many dealers believe this year's slide was exacerbated by speculative funds baling out of oil and commodities after big gains in 1996 and fears of a false start in the global economic recovery.
Monday saw several other commodities including gold, industrial metals led by copper, coffee, cocoa and sugar drifting or tending lower in thin trading.

Traders saw no new big fund sell-offs of the kind seen in recent weeks by the time London markets closed but were wary that funds might have more long positions to liquidate before they consider buying at the lows.
In the short-term, metals and other commodities probably have further to fall as overheated markets correct lower, accentuated by the jitters on Wall Street and firmer interest rates, analysts said.

Nickel and coffee are down around 15 percent from recent highs on fund profit-taking. But some analysts are bullish on industrial metals in the longer term, arguing that higher interest rates only occur when economies are steaming ahead and demand for metals is high.
"The very reason that interest rates are being increased is due to the health of the economy," said analyst Nick Moore of Flemings Global Mining Group.
